verdicts.evidence: The return expression directly calls `fs.existsSync` on the path formed from `packageRoot` and `src` (f1:22-23).

`isSourceCheckout` is true when `fs.existsSync(packageRoot/src)` is true; `inspectContainerBootstrap` then returns `needed: false`, and `runPostinstall` returns when `needed` is false. The install code after that return therefore runs only when the source path does not exist and bootstrap is needed
The test asks whether the `src` path under the package root exists, so `file_or_dir_exists` fits (f1:22-23).
The `prepare` script includes the shell test `test -w .git/config` in its short-circuit command chain (f2:113).
`test -w .git/config` tests whether `.git/config` is writable, not whether it merely exists (f2:113).
The `-w` test checks write permission on `.git/config`, a permission/capability property rather than file or directory existence (f2:113).

The source-checkout early return prevents subsequent inspection, while the `!inspection.needed` early return prevents the bootstrap block; the cited install path is reached only after both return conditions are avoided. Both guards include the absence of the source `src` path (f1:73-97, 171-182).
When the source checkout gate is passed and packaged dependencies are missing, `inspection.needed` is true and the postinstall code calls the dependency bootstrap routine (f1:82-97, 173-182).
The path without a `src` checkout can trigger the packaged dependency installation, while a source checkout returns `needed: false` (f1:73-80, 173-180).

The test explicitly distinguishes a source checkout from the packaged layout, skipping this bootstrap for source trees while enabling it for packaged installs; this is a portability/install-layout purpose rather than an unclear one (f1:73-80, 82-97).

The guarded postinstall block calls `bootstrapContainerDependencies`, whose definition calls `spawnSync`; the dependency inspection also marks the path needed only after the cited source-checkout early return is avoided (f1:73-97, 171-182, 158-168).
`runPostinstall` and `bootstrapContainerDependencies` are exported functions, so callers can invoke the bootstrap path outside the cited gate-controlled call in the script entrypoint (f1:158-182).

The bootstrap wrapper resolves an npm command and passes it to `spawnSync` with install arguments for the container directory, which can install the missing runtime dependencies (f1:100-136, 158-168).
The `&&` chain runs `husky` only if `command -v git` succeeds and `test -w .git/config` succeeds; the cited writeability test is therefore part of the single short-circuit condition (f2:113).
When the command chain succeeds, its final command is `husky`, allowing the package preparation behavior to run (f2:113).
The `husky` command is attempted only when the environment supplies `git` and `.git/config` is writable (f2:113).
The command guards Husky setup on whether this is a Git-capable checkout with writable Git configuration, indicating portability of repository setup rather than an unclear purpose (f2:113).
The successful short-circuit chain reaches the `husky` command at the cited region itself (f2:113).
The package lifecycle script contains this single `husky` command, and the cited region is the command itself with no wrapper function or alternate caller shown in either record file (f2:113).
The final command in the guarded chain invokes `husky`, which is a process execution sink for the guarded repository setup behavior (f2:113).
The existence of the container package manifest decides whether postinstall bootstrap inspection proceeds, so this filesystem check is part of an install-time environment gate (f1:61-71, 171-173).
The existence check on `npm_execpath` helps select between invoking npm through Node and falling back to the `npm` command, so it affects install-time command selection (f1:119-133).
Each missing dependency manifest causes that dependency to be added to the missing list, which later determines whether bootstrap installation is needed (f1:39-57, 82-97).
If the container manifest is absent, dependency names are read as an empty list, changing the subsequent dependency inspection and bootstrap decision (f1:26-31, 39-57, 82-97).
The cited test returns early with no dependency names when the container manifest does not exist, affecting the later install decision (f1:26-31, 39-57, 82-97).
The container manifest existence check gates all later source-checkout and missing-dependency inspection, and thus can decide whether postinstall work runs (f1:61-97, 171-180).
The npm invocation check uses `npm_execpath`, its absolute-path property, and the existence of that path to choose the child command (f1:119-133).
A dependency manifest missing from container `node_modules` is appended to `missing`, which later makes the postinstall bootstrap necessary (f1:39-57, 82-97).
